doc.title: Etta Jones interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998

title: Buddy Johnson's reputation and her good bosses
summary: Johnson was big in the South and major cities; she later worked with him again and says Earl Hines and J.C. Heard were also good bosses.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: He was a guy, Buddy didn’t perhaps get the recognition that he deserved.
Through the south he did. And in New York, and the big cities like Chicago, New York and Philadelphia and those kind of places I think he did. But through the south he was very big.

Was it different, in later years, when you would tour different parts of the country? Were you met with obviously different kinds of audiences, but what was it like being on the road in different areas of the country?

It was just about, well I think a lot of times the south was more, well I was with kind of a blues band I guess, and he was so popular so they were like wonderful. Everywhere he went they greeted him so boisterously. They really liked Buddy Johnson. He was really a big band leader in that time. But a lot of people don’t seem to even remember him or know of him today. But he was a very big band leader.
And you worked on and off with him in later years too.

Yeah. Well we happened to be thrown into the same theater at the same time, but I never was with the band anymore. But we were in Chicago later, after I had “Don’t Go To Strangers,” and we worked together and he was so happy for me, because he was an extremely nice man. I happened to have very nice bosses. Because Earl Hines was wonderful, and J.C. Heard was a wonderful boss for me.
That’s fortunate because it could have gone the other way.
It could have. Because I’ve heard stories that I don’t care to repeat. Some of the band leaders were kind of rough you know. But I always managed to get the nicest, nicest people.
